prompt.context: Our client is the CEO of a major airline company. He has asked us to determine whether or not he should paint his fleet of planes. This is a strategy / qualitative case that also requires some estimation.
prompt.question: Should the airline CEO paint his fleet of planes? Determine the costs and benefits, then assess whether painting makes financial sense.

clarifying_info.q: How much does it cost to paint one plane?
Are there ongoing costs after painting?
clarifying_info.a: Yes — $10,000 per year in additional fuel costs due to added weight.

clarifying_info.q: Does the airline own or lease its planes?
clarifying_info.a: The planes are owned, not leased.

clarifying_info.q: How many planes are in the fleet?
When were the planes last painted?
clarifying_info.a: 5 years ago, which is the industry average interval.

clarifying_info.q: What is the customer base and average ticket price?
clarifying_info.a: 2 million customers per year, average ticket price of $500.

framework: Step 1 — Identify the benefits of painting the planes
Step 2 — Identify the costs of painting the planes
Step 3 — Qualitatively balance costs vs. benefits
Step 4 — Calculate the break-even incremental customers needed to justify the investment and assess reasonableness

questions.prompt: What are the benefits of painting the planes?
questions.guidance: Candidate should brainstorm multiple benefit categories: extended plane life (paint protects the fuselage from corrosion), enhanced branding / brand refresh, potential advertising revenue if exterior space is sold to advertisers, improved premium image which may support higher pricing or attract higher-value customers.

questions.prompt: What are the costs of painting the planes?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify: direct paint and materials cost ($20,000 per plane), labor costs for painting, time each plane is out of service (opportunity cost of lost revenue during downtime), and the ongoing additional annual fuel cost due to added weight ($10,000 per plane per year).

math.setup: Total upfront paint cost = $20,000 x 100 planes. Annual ongoing fuel penalty = $10,000 x 100 planes.
steps: Annual fuel cost = $10,000 x 100 = $1,000,000 per year

questions.prompt: How many additional customers (or revenue uplift) would be needed to break even on the painting investment?
questions.guidance: This is a qualitative / sanity-check calculation. Compare the total incremental costs to the current revenue base to see if the required uplift is feasible. A full break-even would also need to account for the time horizon (e.g., if the paint lasts 5 years, amortize the upfront cost). Candidate should flag that the qualitative benefits (brand image, potential ad revenue) may make a case that the hard numbers alone cannot.

math.setup: Current revenue = 2,000,000 customers x $500 = $1,000,000,000 per year. Year-1 total incremental cost = $2,000,000 (paint) + $1,000,000 (fuel) = $3,000,000. Ongoing annual cost = $1,000,000. Break-even additional customers needed (year 1) at $500/ticket.
steps: Additional customers needed to cover year-1 cost = $3,000,000 / $500 = 6,000 customers
For ongoing annual fuel cost only: $1,000,000 / $500 = 2,000 additional customers per year (0.1% of base)
math.answer: The airline needs roughly 6,000 incremental customers in year 1 (0.3% of current base) to cover the full first-year cost, and only ~2,000 incremental customers per year thereafter. This is a very small hurdle relative to the 2M customer base, suggesting painting is likely worthwhile if there is any meaningful brand or image benefit.

brainstorming.prompt: What other creative considerations or revenue opportunities should the CEO explore when deciding to paint the planes?

categories.name: Revenue opportunities
ideas: Sell exterior fuselage space as advertising to third-party brands
Use new paint scheme to launch a brand refresh or sub-brand
Use distinctive livery as social-media-worthy content to generate organic marketing

categories.name: Cost mitigations
ideas: Negotiate fleet discount with paint supplier for 100-plane order
Schedule painting during low-demand periods to minimize lost revenue
Explore lighter paint formulations to reduce or eliminate fuel penalty

categories.name: Brand and image
ideas: Fresh paint signals modernity and maintenance quality to travelers
Differentiating livery helps stand out in a commoditized market
Improved perceived quality may support a modest price premium

categories.name: Operational factors
ideas: Stagger painting to avoid grounding too many planes simultaneously
Align painting schedule with scheduled maintenance downtime
Evaluate whether paint protects or extends airframe life, reducing long-run maintenance costs

recommendation: Yes, the CEO should paint the fleet. The financial hurdle is very low — only ~0.3% incremental customer growth is needed to break even in year 1 — while the qualitative benefits (brand refresh, potential advertising revenue, improved image, extended airframe protection) are meaningful.
Prioritize scheduling to minimize aircraft downtime and explore lightweight paint options to reduce the ongoing fuel cost penalty.
risks: Fuel cost penalty of $1M/year is ongoing and permanent; if customer uplift does not materialize, this is a recurring drag on margins.
Painting 100 planes requires careful scheduling to avoid operational disruption.
Brand refresh may not resonate if the underlying product quality or service does not improve.
next_steps: Get competitive bids for a 100-plane fleet paint job to validate the $20,000 per plane cost and potentially negotiate a volume discount.
Analyze whether selling advertising space on the fuselage is feasible and what revenue it could generate.
Develop a staggered painting schedule aligned with existing maintenance windows to minimize revenue loss from grounded planes.
